title: Going back when you've broken it
promise: You'll set up your project's undo and rehearse it before you need it: save points, how to go back and how long it takes you. By the end you'll have broken something deliberately and recovered it, timed.
why: Nuria decided to improve her client reminder workflow on a Friday afternoon. She touched three nodes, saved, and it stopped working. She tried Ctrl+Z and the tool no longer remembered. She had no copy. She spent the whole Saturday rebuilding from memory a workflow that had taken her two weeks, and she left it worse than it was. What she needed wasn't more knowledge: it was a five-second copy made before touching anything.

theory.title: The problem isn't breaking it, it's not being able to go back
theory.text: You're going to break things. It's part of working and it can't be avoided: what can be avoided is the damage. The difference between a twenty-minute scare and a lost weekend isn't how serious the breakage is, it's whether you have a point to go back to. And that point has to exist beforehand, because afterwards it can't be created. This is the dullest lesson in the block and the one that will save you most often. The people who work fast and fearlessly aren't the ones who break nothing: they're the ones who know going back costs them one click, and that's why they dare to try things.
theory.analogy: It's the saved game. Without saving, every boss fight is played to the death and you end up avoiding the hard parts. With the save file you go for it, because losing costs three minutes.
theory.example: Nuria: a two-week workflow, a five-minute change, a lost Saturday. With a save point it would have been thirty seconds.

theory.title: Save before, not after
theory.text: The rule is one line: before touching something that works, save a copy. Not when you finish, not when you see it's going well. Before. The reason is that the moment you discover you've broken it is always later than you think, sometimes days later, and by then the good version no longer exists anywhere. And the copy has to be outside the tool you work in, because the most frequent failure isn't you making a mistake: it's the tool eating the previous version, or your account expiring, or a button you thought said duplicate turning out to say replace.
theory.example: A habit that works: the copy's name carries the date and what you were about to change. «reminders-workflow_2026-09-05_before-touching-the-filter.json». It makes sense six months later.

theory.title: How each thing gets saved
theory.text: Every kind of setup gets saved a different way and all of them are easy. An n8n, Make or Zapier workflow gets exported to a file from the workflow's own menu, and that file goes in your folder. A code project or a website gets saved with git, which you already saw with GitHub Desktop: one commit and you have the point. A spreadsheet gets duplicated with the date in the name. And an assistant's instructions, the prompts and the configurations get copied into a text file, which is the part everyone forgets because it doesn't feel like work, right up until it's lost and has to be rewritten from memory.
theory.example: Álvaro saves three things before touching anything: the exported workflow JSON, the file with the assistant's instructions and a screenshot of the configuration screen. Thirty seconds.

theory.title: A copy you've never restored isn't a copy
theory.text: This is the mistake almost everyone discovers at the worst possible moment. You have a saved file, disaster strikes, you try to restore it and it turns out it exported incomplete, or the keys weren't inside, or the tool won't accept that format. A copy only counts as a copy once you've genuinely restored it at least once. The test is done cold, without pressure and with nothing broken: you restore somewhere new, check it works, and now you know your net is in place. And time it, because knowing whether going back costs you two minutes or two hours completely changes the decisions you make.
theory.example: Nuria discovered her n8n exports didn't include the credentials. The copy was fine, but restoring it meant reconnecting five services. She found out in a cold test, not in the disaster.

theory.title: Touch one thing and test
theory.text: Undo is more useful the shorter the jumps are. If you change one thing, test and save, then when something breaks you'll know exactly what it was and you'll go back a single step. If you change fifteen things over two hours and then test, when it fails all you can do is go back to the start and lose the full two hours, the good part included. Small changes with a test in between look slower and are much faster, because you never lose more than one step.
theory.analogy: It's climbing a ladder watching where you put your feet on each rung, instead of taking four at a time. If you trip, you go back one rung and not the whole ladder.
theory.example: Nuria touched three nodes at once. When it failed she didn't know which it was, and going back meant losing everything. With three separate steps she'd have lost one. And there's an effect you notice within a week: when each change comes with its own test, you stop fearing changes. Knowing the worst case is redoing the last ten minutes, you take on things you used to put off.

theory.title: Nothing gets touched on a Friday afternoon
theory.text: This isn't superstition, it's arithmetic. A change made when you're tired, in a hurry to leave and with nobody available if it goes wrong, has every chance of going wrong. And if it breaks, the damage sits there until Monday, which in a business means two days of lost appointments or unanswered clients. The rule everyone who's been burned once uses: changes to something that works get made when you have time ahead of you to fix them, and they get tested the same day. If you only have a few minutes before you leave, save the copy and leave it for tomorrow.
theory.example: Nuria's Friday was five minutes of change and a Saturday of repair. On Monday morning it would have been five minutes of change and twenty of repair.

tasks.title: List what has to be saved
tasks.where: In a file next to your project
tasks.action: Write down everything that makes up your setup and that you'd lose if it disappeared. Think in five categories: the workflows or automations, the code or website if you have one, the spreadsheets and databases, the instructions and prompts, and the configurations (what's connected to what, what warnings you have set). Next to each one write where it lives right now.
tasks.expect: A list of between four and eight things. The usual surprise is the instructions and prompts: hours of work living only inside a text field on another company's website.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know where to start, ask yourself this: if I lost access to this account tomorrow, what would I have to rebuild from scratch? That's exactly the list.

tasks.title: Save a copy of everything, today
tasks.where: In a new folder on your computer
tasks.action: Create a folder with today's date and save a copy of each item on the list inside it. The workflows, exported from the workflow's own menu (look for «Download», «Export» or the three dots). The instructions and prompts, copied into text files. The configurations, with screenshots, which are perfectly fine. The code, with a commit if you use git.
tasks.expect: A dated folder with everything inside. Open it and check the files aren't empty: a zero-byte export is a classic.
tasks.stuck: If your tool won't export, take screenshots of every configuration screen and save the important text in separate files. It isn't as good, but it turns a day of rebuilding into an hour.

tasks.title: Rehearse the restore, cold and timed
tasks.action: This is the task that makes everything before it worth doing. Take the copy of your workflow or setup and restore it as though it were new: in n8n, «Import from file» and create a new workflow; elsewhere, the equivalent. Don't replace the working one, create a new one beside it. Start a timer. Check what's missing when you restore it: almost always the credentials.
tasks.expect: A working duplicate and a time written down. Write in your file: «Going back costs me X minutes and I have to reconnect Y.» That figure is worth its weight in gold and almost nobody has it.
tasks.stuck: If it doesn't work when you restore, better to know today. Note what's missing and adjust how you save: if it's the keys, note in a separate file which services have to be reconnected and at which steps. Never store the keys in the same file as the workflow.

tasks.title: Break something deliberately and recover it
tasks.where: In the duplicate, not the good one
tasks.action: In the duplicated workflow, break something for real: delete two steps, change an important setting, save. Now recover it from your copy. Time it again. This is a fire drill and it's the only way to know your plan works.
tasks.expect: The duplicate back as it was and a second time written down. When it happens for real, you'll have done it once and your hands won't shake.
tasks.stuck: If you get in a tangle, that's exactly the information you were after: it means your way of saving is too complicated. Simplify it until restoring is opening a file and pressing import.

tasks.title: Write your undo plan
tasks.action: Five lines, written for you in six months and in a hurry: where the copies are, how each kind of thing gets restored (with the button name), what has to be reconnected afterwards, how long it takes, and how often you'll make a fresh copy. Save it in the same folder as the copies.
tasks.expect: Five lines you could follow on a day when you're rattled. Read them aloud: if any of them makes you stop and think, rewrite it simpler.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know how often to make copies, use this rule: always before touching anything, and once a month even if you touch nothing. Put the reminder in your calendar, because «when I remember» means never.

tasks.title: Get your plan reviewed
tasks.action: Give it your list of what you save and your plan, and ask it to find the holes. It's very good at spotting what you forgot to save.
tasks.prompt:
I have a setup built without programming using [TOOLS: n8n, spreadsheets, an assistant with instructions, whatever] and I've prepared a backup.

WHAT I SAVE:
[YOUR LIST]

MY PLAN FOR GOING BACK:
[YOUR FIVE LINES]

Review it as though you had to use it in an emergency:
1. What I forgot to save and would notice missing when restoring. Be specific: name the item.
2. Which step of my plan would fail if I did it in a hurry and rattled.
3. One thing I'd remove from the plan for being unnecessary.

Don't give me a new plan or general best practices. Just the holes in mine.
tasks.expect: Two or three things you hadn't saved. The most typical: environment variables, permissions on shared folders, and which account is connected to what.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with a backup manual, cut it short: «I don't want theory. Tell me which specific item on my list is missing.»

matters: That the save point gets created before touching anything, because afterwards it can't be.
That a copy you've never restored doesn't count as a copy.
That instructions and prompts are hours of work almost nobody saves.
That small changes with a test in between mean you never lose more than one step.
ignore: Automated backup systems with versioning. At your scale a folder with dates is plenty.
Storing keys inside the copies. Never, and least of all if they go to a shared folder.
Saving every hour. Before touching and once a month is enough.
canDo: Get back to how things were before your last change.
Know how long recovery takes you, because you've timed it.
Discover today that your copy was incomplete, rather than in the disaster.
Dare to try things, because going back no longer frightens you.
cantDo: Go back in tools that won't export, beyond screenshots.
Recover data deleted in someone else's service.
Skip the restore test and trust it anyway.
words: The copy made before touching something that worked. The only thing that lets you go back.
Getting a workflow or configuration out into a file you can keep outside the tool.
Testing the recovery when nothing is broken, to find out whether it really works.
The save point in git, for code and websites. You make one when something works.
The keys and connections to other services. They almost never come inside the export: they get reconnected separately.
next: You can go back now. In lesson 38 you build what you need in order not to have to keep watching: warnings that tell you something has stopped, without opening the tool every morning.
